questions.q: What are the three paths to getting a model into production, as described in this lesson?
options: Self-hosted, cloud AI platform, and fully managed SaaS
questions.explain: The three paths are self-hosting on your own GPUs, using a cloud AI platform behind an API, or buying a fully managed SaaS product built on a model.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four things a cloud AI platform bundles for you?
options: Guaranteed model accuracy for your specific use case
questions.explain: A cloud AI platform gives you compute, a model catalog, governance, and consolidated billing — but it never guarantees accuracy for your specific use case; that still depends on your data and evaluation.

questions.q: In the self-hosted code example, what does the engineer have to manage that disappears when using a cloud AI platform?
options: Loading the model file and running the serving process
The content of the AI's reply
questions.explain: Self-hosted code loads and serves the model directly. On a cloud AI platform, that work is replaced by a client call to a managed endpoint.

questions.q: Which billing model is typical of a cloud AI platform, as opposed to self-hosting?
options: Pay-per-token or pay-per-deployment-hour instead of owning depreciating hardware
A flat annual fee regardless of usage
questions.explain: Cloud AI platforms typically bill by usage — tokens processed or deployment-hours — rather than requiring you to buy and depreciate GPU hardware.

questions.q: Where does this course focus, among the three paths to production?
options: The cloud AI platform path — building against a managed model layer
None of the three; it focuses purely on model training
questions.explain: This course centers on the cloud AI platform path, since that's where most AI engineering roles sit: building real applications against a managed model layer like Azure AI Foundry.
